ticket_data.title: StepValueValidator accepts invalid values and crashes on large numbers
ticket_data.description:
`StepValueValidator` uses `math.remainder()`. That converts values to float. Large integers and Decimals lose precision or crash.

{{{#!python
from decimal import Decimal
from django import forms

forms.IntegerField(step_size=2).clean("9007199254740993")
# Returns 9007199254740993. It is odd, so it should be rejected.

forms.IntegerField(step_size=2).clean("9" * 400)
# OverflowError: int too large to convert to float

forms.DecimalField(step_size=Decimal("0.1")).clean("1e400")
# ValueError: math domain error

forms.DecimalField(step_size=Decimal("0.01")).clean("12345678901234567.01")
# ValidationError, but the value is a valid multiple of 0.01
}}}

The first case lets an invalid value through. The next two raise an unhandled exception, so user input can cause a 500 error.

Floats are also used for the tolerance (`abs_tol=1e-9`). So `Decimal("1.00000000005")` is accepted with a step of `Decimal("1e-10")`.

I think int and Decimal values should be checked with exact arithmetic. The float path can stay as it is. Be careful not to turn the Decimal into a huge number: `Fraction(Decimal("1e50000000"))` takes about a minute.

I am happy to work on a patch once this is accepted.

ticket_data.title: Drop support for Python 3.12 & 3.13
ticket_data.description:
Django 6.2 LTS, supported until April 2030, is the last version to support:
- Python 3.12 (end of life: October 2028)
- Python 3.13 (end of life: October 2029)

Per [https://github.com/django/deps/blob/main/accepted/0020-annual-release-cycle.rst DEP 20], each feature release supports the two Python versions receiving bug fixes at the start of its pre-release phase, plus the most recent one to have moved to security fixes only. Django 2028 therefore supports Python 3.14, 3.15, and 3.16.

See [https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/dev/faq/install/#what-python-version-can-i-use-with-django our policy about Python version support]. For Django 2028, the dates work out like this:

- Django 2028 is released in January 2028 and reaches end of life in December 2030.
- Python 3.14, its oldest supported Python, was released in October 2025 and gets five years of upstream support, so it reaches end of life in October 2030.

The same holds every year: Django 2029 supports 3.15 through 3.17, and 3.15 reaches end of life in October 2031, two months before 2029 does in December 2031.

ticket_data.title: order_by("pk") on a union() of a composite pk model crashes or sorts wrongly
ticket_data.description:
{{{#!python
class Comment(models.Model):
    pk = models.CompositePrimaryKey("tenant_id", "comment_id")
    tenant_id = models.IntegerField()
    comment_id = models.IntegerField()

# rows (tenant_id, comment_id): (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 1)
qs = Comment.objects.filter(tenant_id=1).union(Comment.objects.filter(tenant_id=2))
}}}

Ordering a combined query by a composite primary key fails in two ways.

1. On a normal queryset, `order_by("pk")` crashes. `first()` crashes too, because it orders by `pk`.

{{{#!python
qs.first()
qs.order_by("pk")  # when evaluated
# TypeError: 'NoneType' object does not support item assignment
}}}

The error is raised in `Query.add_select_col()` (called from `SQLCompiler.get_order_by()`), because `query.selected` is `None`.

2. With `values_list("pk")` there is no error, but the order is wrong.

{{{#!python
list(qs.values_list("pk").order_by("pk"))
# [((1, 1),), ((2, 1),), ((1, 2),)]
# expected: [((1, 1),), ((1, 2),), ((2, 1),)]
}}}

The SQL ends with `ORDER BY "col1"`, and `col1` is only the last pk column (`comment_id`). The same query without `union()` is ordered correctly.

I think `get_order_by()` treats the composite pk (`ColPairs`) as a single column in the combinator branch. It should order by each column of the pk.

Related: #36065, #37354 (other composite pk ordering bugs).

    self.assertEqual(quote_lexeme(lexeme), quoted)
                     ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/django/contrib/postgres/search.py", line 26, in quote_lexeme
    return UTF8Dumper(str).quote(psql_escape(value)).decode()
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/psycopg/adapt.py", line 59, in quote
    if (value := self.dump(obj)) is None:
                 ~~~~~~~~~^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/django/contrib/postgres/search.py", line 23, in dump

ticket_data.title: No system check for GenericRelation on a model with DB_CASCADE, leaving orphaned generic rows
ticket_data.description:
The docs say that database-level and Python-level `on_delete` variants cannot be mixed in the same model or in related models. System checks enforce this with `models.E050` and `fields.E323`.

`GenericRelation` is a Python-level cleanup, but it is not checked. If a model has a `GenericRelation` and a `DB_CASCADE` foreign key, the database deletes the model's rows and Django never deletes the generic related objects. They stay in the table with no error and no check warning.

{{{#!python
class Tag(models.Model):
    content_type = models.ForeignKey(ContentType, models.CASCADE)
    object_id = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    content_object = GenericForeignKey()


class Author(models.Model):
    pass


class Book(models.Model):
    author = models.ForeignKey(Author, models.DB_CASCADE)
    tags = GenericRelation(Tag)
}}}

{{{#!python
>>> author = Author.objects.create()
>>> book = Book.objects.create(author=author)
>>> book.tags.create()
>>> author.delete()
>>> Book.objects.count(), Tag.objects.count()
(0, 1)
}}}

`manage.py check` reports no issues. With `models.CASCADE` instead of `models.DB_CASCADE`, the `Tag` row is deleted.

Why it happens: `Collector.collect()` skips `DB_CASCADE` relations, so `Book` instances are never collected. Their private fields are never visited, so `GenericRelation.bulk_related_objects()` never runs. `GenericRelation.remote_field.on_delete` is `DO_NOTHING`, so `Model._check_related_fields()` does not see it as a Python-level variant.

I verified this on 6.1.3 and on main with SQLite. I also ran random schemas with database and Python `on_delete` variants against the equivalent all-Python schemas. Among schemas that pass all checks, the only difference in the final data was orphaned generic rows.

Suggested fix: add a system check error for a model that has a `GenericRelation` (any private field with `bulk_related_objects()`) and a `DB_CASCADE` foreign key. It would not fire for `DB_SET_NULL` or `DB_SET_DEFAULT`, because those do not delete the model's rows. This is the same kind of gap as #37254 (implicit M2M through tables), which was fixed in 6.1.x.

I am happy to work on a patch once the approach is agreed.

ticket_data.title: Database session backends crash on session keys containing a null character
ticket_data.description:
A request with the header {{{Cookie: sessionid="AAAAAAAA\000"}}} (printable ASCII only) returns HTTP 500 when using the {{{db}}} or {{{cached_db}}} session backend on PostgreSQL.

{{{http.cookies}}} unquotes the {{{\000}}} escape into a null character. {{{SessionBase._validate_session_key()}}} accepts the key, because it checks only {{{key and len(key) >= 8}}}. {{{SessionStore._get_session_from_db()}}} (and {{{_aget_session_from_db()}}}) then passes it to the database. PostgreSQL's driver rejects it (psycopg 3 raises {{{DataError}}}, psycopg2 raises {{{ValueError}}}), and the exception propagates out of {{{SessionMiddleware}}}. Because the session loads in middleware, every URL is affected, and the 500 response doesn't clear the cookie, so a client holding it keeps getting 500s until the cookie is removed.

The {{{cache}}}, {{{file}}} and {{{signed_cookies}}} backends, and the {{{db}}} backend on SQLite, return 200 for the same cookie.

To reproduce, save the script below as {{{poc.py}}}, then run these commands in the same directory. They need Docker and Python 3.12 or later; the container is removed on stop.

{{{#!sh
python3 -m venv djnul-venv
. djnul-venv/bin/activate
docker run --rm -d --name djnul -e POSTGRES_DB=djnul -e POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust -p 55432:5432 postgres:17
until docker exec djnul pg_isready -h localhost -U postgres -q; do sleep 1; done
pip install "Django>=6.0,<6.1" "psycopg[binary]"
PGHOST=localhost PGPORT=55432 PGUSER=postgres python poc.py
docker stop djnul
}}}

It prints {{{crafted: 500}}} and {{{normal: 200}}}. To test main instead, install {{{git+https://github.com/django/django.git}}} in place of the Django release. The script sets only the database {{{NAME}}}, so psycopg picks up the host, port and user from the {{{PG*}}} environment variables.

{{{#!python
import django
from django.conf import settings

settings.configure(
    DEBUG=False,
    ALLOWED_HOSTS=["testserver"],
    SECRET_KEY="x",
    DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql", "NAME": "djnul"}},
    INSTALLED_APPS=["django.contrib.contenttypes", "django.contrib.auth", "django.contrib.sessions"],
    MIDDLEWARE=["django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware"],
    ROOT_URLCONF="__main__",
)
django.setup()

from django.core.management import call_command
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.test import Client
from django.urls import path

def view(request):
    request.session.get("x")
    return HttpResponse("ok")

urlpatterns = [path("", view)]

call_command("migrate", run_syncdb=True, verbosity=0)
client = Client(raise_request_exception=False)
print("crafted:", client.get("/", HTTP_COOKIE='sessionid="AAAAAAAA\\000"').status_code)  # 500
print("normal: ", client.get("/", HTTP_COOKIE="sessionid=" + "a" * 32).status_code)  # 200
}}}

Tested on Django 6.0.9 and main, with psycopg 3 and psycopg2. The code is the same on 5.2, 6.0, 6.1 and main.

Proposed fix: make {{{_validate_session_key()}}} also reject keys containing a null character, so such a key becomes "no session", the same as an unknown key. Restricting keys to {{{VALID_KEY_CHARS}}} (as the file backend does) would be stricter, but it would break the {{{signed_cookies}}} backend, whose keys are signed strings containing {{{:}}}, {{{-}}}, {{{_}}} and uppercase letters.

This was first reported to security@djangoproject.com, and the security team asked for a public ticket.

I prepared this report and patch with help from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) via Claude Code, and I reviewed and verified the output myself.

ticket_data.title: Run async signal receivers sequentially
ticket_data.description:
Since async signal support was added, `Signal.send()` and `Signal.asend()` run async receivers concurrently. This causes two problems:

 * '''Registration order is lost.''' In sync Django, receivers run in the order they were registered, and projects often rely on this for good reasons. With async receivers, the order is lost silently, so converting a receiver from sync to async can change behavior.
 * '''Transactions inside receivers are not well ordered.''' Since each receiver runs in its own task, their queries and savepoints can interleave. This came up in the review of async `transaction.atomic()` (#33882, [https://github.com/django/django/pull/22074 PR #22074]): receivers can't use `atomic()` inside an async transaction, and inside a sync transaction a write from one receiver can be silently rolled back with another receiver's savepoint.

'''Proposal:''' await async receivers one by one, in registration order, in the caller's task. This keeps the same semantics as sync receivers and makes transaction handling inside receivers safe.

'''Trade-off:''' slow receivers would no longer run concurrently. This is a behavior change and would need a release note.

ticket_data.title: Test client responses form a reference cycle via `response.json` and need a GC pass to be freed
ticket_data.description:
`Client.request()` and `AsyncClient.request()` attach a `json` helper to every response as {{{#!python response.json = partial(self._parse_json, response) }}} ([https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/test/client.py#L1132 client.py#L1132], [https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/test/client.py#L1524 #L1524]). The `partial` holds a strong reference to the response and is stored on the response itself, so every response returned by the test client is part of a reference cycle. Reference counting can never free it; it survives until the cyclic garbage collector runs. Because the response also holds `response.templates`, `response.context` (every `Context`/`RequestContext` rendered during the request), `response.request`, `response.wsgi_request` and the rendered content, the whole graph stays alive with it. This is the same class of problem as #36701 (`ModelState` cycles), which was accepted and fixed. === Impact === On a large suite (~11k tests, many of them making admin requests) this was the main source of cyclic garbage. With Python 3.14.0–3.14.4 (incremental GC, reverted in 3.14.5) the garbage was collected much more slowly than it was produced: a single pytest-xdist worker grew from ~360 MB to ~1.8 GB over 1266 tests, and `-n auto` on a 14-core / 14 GB machine exhausted RAM. With the generational GC the garbage does get collected, but every test-client response still has to be reclaimed by a gen-2 pass instead of being freed on `del`, which means extra GC work and a higher memory peak in long suites. === Reproduction (standalone, no project needed) === {{{#!python import gc import django from django.conf import settings settings.configure( ROOT_URLCONF=__name__, ALLOWED_HOSTS=["testserver"], SECRET_KEY="x", TEMPLATES=[{"BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates"}], ) django.setup() from django.http import HttpResponse from django.template import engines from django.test import Client from django.test.utils import setup_test_environment from django.urls import path def view(request): tpl = engines["django"].from_string("{% for i in r %}

{{ i }}

{% endfor %}") return HttpResponse(tpl.render({"r": range(50)})) urlpatterns = [path("", view)] setup_test_environment() c = Client() c.get("/") gc.disable() gc.collect() r = c.get("/") del r print("objects in cycles after one request:", gc.collect()) # 71 r = c.get("/") del r.json del r print("same, after removing response.json:", gc.collect()) # 0 }}} Output (Django 5.2.19 and main, Python 3.14.9; same on 3.14.4): {{{ objects in cycles after one request: 71 same, after removing response.json: 0 }}} `response.json` is the only cycle. Once it is removed, nothing is left for the collector. === Possible fix === Keep a weak reference to the response in the helper: {{{#!python response.json = partial(self._parse_json, weakref.proxy(response)) }}} (in both `Client.request()` and `AsyncClient.request()`). `response.json()` keeps working, and the parsed result is still cached on `response._json` (#27516). With this change the reproduction above reports `0` objects in cycles. The only behaviour change is that calling a detached `json` after the response itself has been released raises `ReferenceError`, e.g. `f = client.get(...).json; f()`. That seems unlikely in practice. If it matters, `json` could instead be exposed through a small descriptor. A regression test could assert that, with `gc.disable()`, a response from `client.get()` is freed as soon as it is deleted. For example, take a `weakref.ref(response)`, then `del response`, and check that the ref is `None` without calling `gc.collect()`.

ticket_data.title: Avoid importing ctypes at import time in django.core.files.locks on Windows
ticket_data.description:
On Windows, django/core/files/locks.py imports ctypes and ctypes.wintypes and defines the OVERLAPPED structure and the LockFileEx/UnlockFileEx prototypes at module level. The module is imported by django.core.cache.backends.filebased, which django.core.checks imports, so every `import django.db.models` on Windows imports ctypes and loads _ctypes.pyd, libffi and the OLE DLLs _ctypes links against, whether or not anything ever locks a file. On other platforms the module only imports fcntl.

Measured on Windows 11 with Python 3.14.4 and Django main (8e3dec6):

- `python -X importtime -c "import django.db.models"`: django.core.files.locks takes 11.2 ms cumulative on Windows (0.1 ms on Linux, same machine under WSL2).
- Building the ctypes objects on the first lock()/unlock() call instead: `import django.db.models` is 6.0 ms faster (310.7 -> 300.9 ms, 95% CI 1.2-13.6 ms, 60 alternating runs timed inside the process).

The constants and the lock/unlock functions stay at module level, so the public behavior is unchanged. `runtests.py files cache file_storage` passes on Windows with the change.

I'd be happy to submit the patch.

AI disclosure: the patch was prepared with GitHub Copilot (Claude Opus 5.5 model), which was used to find the import, and write the patch.

ticket_data.title: set_cookie() ignores the cookie flags required by name prefixes and SameSite=None
ticket_data.description:
`HttpResponse.set_cookie()` emits the `secure` and `httponly` values exactly as it receives them, while
`HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` already applies the flags a browser requires before it stores a cookie.
The result is a syntactically valid `Set-Cookie` header that the browser silently discards.

This affects three documented cases:

|| Cookie name / parameters || Required by the browser || Emitted by set_cookie() ||
|| `__Secure-x`, `__Host-x`, `__Http-x` || `Secure` || nothing, unless the caller passes `secure=True` ||
|| `__Http-x`, `__Host-Http-x` || `HttpOnly` || nothing, unless the caller passes `httponly=True` ||
|| `samesite="None"` || `Secure` || nothing ||

References: RFC 6265bis section 4.1.3 (cookie name prefixes) and the SameSite=None requirements. The
`__Http-` and `__Host-Http-` prefixes come from CHIPS; `delete_cookie()` already handles them, so the
inconsistency is inside the same class.

The failure is silent. The response is a normal 200 with a `Set-Cookie` header, the browser drops the
cookie, and the following request arrives without it. A project that sets
`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME = "__Host-sessionid"` and keeps `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False` (local development,
or TLS terminated in a reverse proxy) sees a successful login followed by a request with no session, and
nothing appears in the server logs.

Steps to reproduce, current behavior:

{{{
>>> from django.http import HttpResponse
>>> r = HttpResponse()
>>> r.set_cookie("__Host-sessionid", "abc")
>>> r.cookies["__Host-sessionid"]["secure"]
''
>>> r.set_cookie("c", "abc", samesite="None")
>>> r.cookies["c"]["secure"]
''
}}}

Expected behavior: `secure` is `True` in both cases, because a browser will not store either cookie
otherwise. Cookies without a name prefix and without `SameSite=None` must keep behaving exactly as
before, with the flags the caller passed and nothing else.

Proposed fix: a module-level helper in `django/http/response.py` that computes the flags required by the
name and by `samesite`, used by both `set_cookie()` and `delete_cookie()` so the two paths cannot
diverge again. The helper only adds flags a browser already requires for that cookie; it never removes
one.

Patch: https://github.com/django/django/pull/22261 (branch `set-cookie-required-flags`), with four
regression tests in `tests/responses/test_cookie.py` and a paragraph in
`docs/ref/request-response.txt`.

Verification:

{{{
$ python tests/runtests.py responses --parallel 1     # with the patch
Ran 61 tests
OK (skipped=1)

$ python tests/runtests.py responses --parallel 1     # django/http/response.py reverted
FAILED (failures=7, skipped=1)
}}}

The seven failures are exactly the new assertions (the prefixed-name loops count one subtest each), so
they measure the change and not the environment.

Not covered by this patch: `__Host-` also requires `Path=/` and no `Domain` attribute. Enforcing that
means changing the contract of `set_cookie()` or adding a `security.W0xx` deployment check that reads
`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` / `CSRF_COOKIE_NAME`; it can be a follow-up rather than part of this diff.

I searched the existing tickets for cookie prefixes, `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite`. The open ones I
found, including 34613 (`Partitioned` support) and the older cookie parsing tickets, do not cover
`set_cookie()` applying the flags required by name prefixes or by `SameSite=None`.

ticket_data.title: makemessages fails to extract context from multiline translation tags
ticket_data.description:
The `makemessages` command doesn't correctly extract contextual translations from multiline `{% translate %}` and `{% blocktranslate %}` template tags.

For example:

{{{
{% blocktranslate
    with name=user.name
    context "greeting"
%}
    Hello {{ name }}
{% endblocktranslate %}
}}}

The template parser correctly recognizes the message context at runtime. However, the extraction logic in `django/utils/translation/template.py` doesn't recognize contexts spanning multiple lines because the regular expressions used for parsing translation tags don't match newline characters.

Consequently, `makemessages` may extract the message without its context, producing an incorrect gettext entry. This is inconsistent with the contextual translation lookup performed at runtime.

There is also a source-location issue. Newlines inside multiline template tags aren't preserved in the output generated by `templatize()`. As a result, subsequent messages can receive incorrect line numbers in generated `.po` files.

This can also affect the association of translator comments with extracted messages.

== Proposed fix ==

The regular expressions used for extracting translation contexts should support multiline tags.

Additionally, the original newlines inside template tags should be preserved during templatization so that gettext receives accurate source locations.

Regression tests should cover:

- Multiline `{% translate %}` tags with message contexts.
- Multiline `{% blocktranslate %}` tags with message contexts.
- Correct extraction of contextual message IDs.
- Preservation of source line numbers after multiline tags.

The issue can be reproduced using `templatize()` directly, and the proposed changes include regression tests covering the affected extraction behavior.

ticket_data.title: Conditional request handling treats the Unix epoch as a missing date
ticket_data.description:
`parse_http_date_safe()` returns `0` for `Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT`, and the conditional request code checks these timestamps for truthiness, so the epoch is handled as if the date were missing:

 * `get_conditional_response()` ignores `If-Unmodified-Since: Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT`, so a request that should get 412 (for any resource modified after 1970) goes through.
 * `_if_unmodified_since_passes()` and `_if_modified_since_passes()` treat a resource whose `Last-Modified` is the epoch as having no modification date: `If-Unmodified-Since` always gives 412, and `If-Modified-Since` never gives 304.
 * `ConditionalGetMiddleware` passes an epoch `Last-Modified` on as missing, and skips conditional handling altogether when the response has no `ETag`.
 * `@condition` / `@last_modified` don't add the `Last-Modified` header when `last_modified_func` returns the epoch.

An epoch `Last-Modified` can come up for files whose mtime was normalized to 0, e.g. by a reproducible build.

Comparing with `is None` / `is not None` instead fixes all four. I have a patch with tests ready.

This touches the same helper as #37252 ([https://github.com/django/django/pull/21737 PR 21737]), where `not last_modified` would also treat the epoch as missing. The two fixes are compatible, and I'm happy to rebase on whichever lands first.

ticket_data.title: GeometryField crashes with RecursionError on deeply nested GeoJSON
ticket_data.description:
The `ExternalCRSBlocker.check()` added for CVE-2026-111362 (ecb2b77b49) parses GeoJSON input with `json.loads()` and doesn't catch `RecursionError`. When the input is nested more deeply than the recursion limit, e.g. a Point with 100,000 nested `[` in `coordinates`, `forms.GeometryField.clean()` raises `RecursionError` (HTTP 500) instead of a `ValidationError`. This also applies to the default widget and the admin. `BaseGeometryWidget.deserialize()` only catches `GEOSException`, `GDALException`, `ValueError` and `TypeError`.

On 6.1.2 the same input gives "Invalid geometry value.", so this is a regression in 6.1.3, and presumably 6.0.10 and 5.2.19 too, since the fix was backported.

```python
from django.contrib.gis import forms
n = 100_000
forms.GeometryField().clean('{"type": "Point", "coordinates": ' + "[" * n + "]" * n + "}")
# 6.1.2: ValidationError; 6.1.3 / main: RecursionError
```

Patch: in `ExternalCRSBlocker.check()`, re-raise `RecursionError` from `json.loads()` as a `ValueError`, so that it's handled like the `JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError` subclass) that callers already handle. Like #37418, the test mocks `json.loads()`, because the depth at which it raises depends on the interpreter's stack size.

ticket_data.title: GeometryField.to_python() crashes with GDALException on invalid GeoJSON when the widget has no deserialize()
ticket_data.description:
#29978 made `GeometryField.to_python()` catch `GDALException` from `widget.deserialize()`. However, when the widget has no `deserialize()` method (e.g. `widget=forms.TextInput`, which `test_field_with_text_widget` covers), `to_python()` calls `GEOSGeometry()` directly and only catches `GEOSException`, `ValueError` and `TypeError`. from django import forms as django_forms

ticket_data.title: makemigrations generates wrong dependencies when a new model has an FK to a renamed model in a different app
ticket_data.description:
When adding a new model with a ForeignKey to a model that is also being renamed in a different app, `makemigrations` generates dependencies that put the new model with a FK to renamed model's new name before renaming the referenced model and `migrate` fails.


1. App `shop` has `class T0(models.Model): pass`. Run `makemigrations`.
{{{#!console
Migrations for 'shop':
  shop/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model T0
}}}
2. Rename `T0` to `T0r`, and add app `zeta` with:
{{{#!python
class T1(models.Model):
    t0 = models.ForeignKey("shop.T0r", models.CASCADE)
}}}
3. Run `makemigrations` and answer yes to the rename.
{{{#!console
Migrations for 'zeta':
  zeta/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model T1
Migrations for 'shop':
  shop/migrations/0002_rename_t0_t0r.py
    ~ Rename model T0 to T0r
}}}
4. Run `migrate`.

The dependencies come out backwards. `shop/0002_rename_t0_t0r` depends on `('zeta', '0001_initial')`, and `zeta/0001_initial` depends only on `('shop', '0001_initial')` even though its foreign key points at `shop.t0r`:

{{{#!console
Applying zeta.0001_initial...
ValueError: Related model 'shop.t0r' cannot be resolved
}}}

This is a regression in Django 2.0 introduced by #28493's change to `generate_renamed_models()`. The same steps work on 1.11 and fail on 2.0 and later. This is essentially the reverse structure of #28493: its foreign key used the old name and had to run before the rename. Here it uses the new name and has to run after.

Changing the dependency in `zeta.0001_initial` to `shop.0002_rename_t0_t0r` and removing the `zeta.0001_initial` dependency from `shop.0002_rename_t0_t0r` makes it work. That's the order generated by Django 1.11, and the only order that works migrating forwards and back.

I haven't had time to investigate further, but I played around a little bit with this patch and it appears to work:

{{{#!diff
diff --git a/django/db/migrations/autodetector.py b/django/db/migrations/autodetector.py
index 907988d..df0a9ef 100644
--- a/django/db/migrations/autodetector.py
+++ b/django/db/migrations/autodetector.py
@@ -596,12 +596,19 @@ class MigrationAutodetector:
                             rem_model_state, model_state
                         ):
                             dependencies = []
+                            # A relation to the old name must be created
+                            # before the rename. A relation added in this run
+                            # refers to the new name and is created after it.
+                            old_relations = self.from_state.relations.get(
+                                (rem_app_label, rem_model_name), {}
+                            )
                             fields = list(model_state.fields.values()) + [
                                 field.remote_field
-                                for relations in self.to_state.relations[
+                                for related_key, relations in self.to_state.relations[
                                     app_label, model_name
-                                ].values()
-                                for field in relations.values()
+                                ].items()
+                                for field_name, field in relations.items()
+                                if field_name in old_relations.get(related_key, {})
                             ]
                             for field in fields:
                                 if field.is_relation:
}}}

I found this with the same fuzzer as #37493, which tests a migration extension that manages database views with Django migrations. Its random changes include renaming a model and adding a model with a foreign key to an existing one, across multiple apps. One change it produced failed to migrate. I then produced a minimal repro using Django alone.

This looks semi-related to #37477, but the proposed patch only applies to changes in a single app at a time.

ticket_data.title: makemigrations --update produces migrations with dependencies that don't exist
ticket_data.description:
`makemigrations --update` generates ephemeral migrations that get merged into each app's last migration. If one run produces new migrations in two apps and one depends on the other, the merged migration keeps the dependency on the ephemeral migration's name, which no longer exists after the merge. `migrate` then fails with `NodeNotFoundError`. I reproduced on 5.2, 6.1 and master.

1. Two apps with one model each. Run `makemigrations`.
{{{#!console
Migrations for 'reports':
  reports/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Report
Migrations for 'shop':
  shop/migrations/0001_initial.py
    + Create model Product
}}}
2. Add `Region` to `reports` and a foreign key to it on `shop.Product`:
{{{#!python
class Region(models.Model):
    pass
}}}
{{{#!python
class Product(models.Model):
    region = models.ForeignKey("reports.Region", models.CASCADE, null=True)
}}}
3. Run `makemigrations --update`.
{{{#!console
Migrations for 'reports':
  reports/migrations/0001_initial_updated.py
    + Create model Report
    + Create model Region
Deleted reports/migrations/0001_initial.py
Migrations for 'shop':
  shop/migrations/0001_initial_updated.py
    + Create model Product
Deleted shop/migrations/0001_initial.py
}}}
4. Run `migrate`.
{{{#!console
django.db.migrations.exceptions.NodeNotFoundError: Migration shop.0001_initial_updated dependencies reference nonexistent parent node ('reports', '0002_region')
}}}

`shop/0001_initial_updated.py` has:
{{{#!python
    dependencies = [
        ('reports', '0002_region'),
    ]
}}}
`reports.0002_region` was the ephemeral migration before the merge, never written to disk. The correct dependency is `reports.0001_initial_updated`. Without `--update`, the same change produces `reports.0002_region` and `shop.0002_product_region` with the right dependency, and `migrate` works.

It doesn't need a new model on the other side. A new foreign key from `shop.Product` to the existing `reports.Report` does the same thing if `reports` has any change at all in the same run, because `makemigrations` makes the new `shop` migration depend on the newest `reports` migration from that run, and `--update` merges that one away too.

The cause is in `write_to_last_migration_files()`. It refuses to update a migration that a migration on disk depends on, but a new migration from the same run is not on disk yet. When new migrations in two apps depend on each other, the dependency is copied onto the merged migration under the ephemeral migration's name, which is never written to disk.

The existing check catches the same dependency once it is on disk. Starting from the two migrations plain `makemigrations` produces in step 2, a change to `reports` alone is refused:
{{{#!console
CommandError: Cannot update migration 'reports.0002_region' that migrations 'shop.0002_product_region' depend on.
}}}


I haven't had too much time to investigate further, but played around with this patch that points dependencies on merged migrations at the migration they were merged into, and refuses an app with more than one new migration. It fixes the steps above on master, and refuses when a cycle would result before deleting anything:

{{{#!diff
--- a/django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py
+++ b/django/core/management/commands/makemigrations.py
@@ -268,6 +268,14 @@
         new_changes = {}
         update_previous_migration_paths = {}
         for app_label, app_migrations in changes.items():
+            # More than one new migration in an app means the changes have a
+            # dependency cycle through another app. Merged into one
+            # migration per app the cycle comes back.
+            if len(app_migrations) > 1:
+                raise CommandError(
+                    f"Cannot update last migration of app {app_label}: its changes "
+                    f"need {len(app_migrations)} migrations."
+                )
             # Find last migration.
             leaf_migration_nodes = loader.graph.leaf_nodes(app=app_label)
             if len(leaf_migration_nodes) == 0:
@@ -332,6 +340,19 @@
             new_changes[app_label] = [leaf_migration]
             update_previous_migration_paths[app_label] = previous_migration_path

+        # A dependency on a migration merged in this run points at the
+        # migration it was merged into.
+        merged = {
+            (app_label, migration.name): (app_label, new_changes[app_label][0].name)
+            for app_label, app_migrations in changes.items()
+            for migration in app_migrations
+        }
+        for [leaf_migration] in new_changes.values():
+            leaf_migration.dependencies = [
+                merged.get(dependency, dependency)
+                for dependency in leaf_migration.dependencies
+            ]
+
         self.write_migration_files(new_changes, update_previous_migration_paths)

     def write_migration_files(self, changes, update_previous_migration_paths=None):
}}}

I found this with the same fuzzer as #37493 and #37495. It runs `makemigrations --update` on random model changes across several apps in order to assert that applying migrations generated with `--update` has the same effect as generating new ones without `--update`. Any change with new migrations in two apps that depend on each other fails this way.

ticket_data.title: Improve GEOSGeometry.tuple performance
ticket_data.description:
In [https://github.com/django/django/pull/22262 PR], David has a proof of concept for improving the performance of the `GEOSGeometry.tuple` property for geometries with many coordinates, from 1.4x - 46x faster depending on the number of coordinates.

Addressing this will make it more practical to use this property when rearchitecting some other geometry construction paths in GeoDjango.

----

Using one of the fixtures (a Polygon, with 799 coords in one coordinate sequence) from the test suite.

Set up
{{{#!py
In [1]: from django.contrib.gis.gdal import DataSource
  ...: from django.contrib.gis.geos import GEOSGeometry
  ...: 
  ...: source = DataSource("tests/gis_tests/data/counties/counties.shp")
  ...: geometry = GEOSGeometry(memoryview(source[0][1].geom.wkb))
}}}

Current

{{{#!py
In [3]: %timeit geometry.tuple
3.4 ms ± 35.7 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
}}}

Proposed

{{{#!py
In [3]: %timeit geometry.tuple
73.2 μs ± 406 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000 loops each)
}}}

A ~46x speedup.

This is a favourable example as it is a single 'large' geometry. The impact will vary depending upon the geometry. A collection of many geometries with each with a small number of coordinates, would perform differently. For example this item from the test suite has 9 sub-geometries with 21 points.

{{{#!py
In [1]: import json
  ...: from pathlib import Path
  ...: from django.contrib.gis.geos import GEOSGeometry
  ...: 
  ...: data = json.loads(
  ...:     Path("tests/gis_tests/data/geometries.json").read_text()
  ...: )
  ...: geometry = GEOSGeometry(data["multilinestrings"][1]["wkt"])
}}}

Current

{{{#!py
In [3]: %timeit geometry.tuple
306 μs ± 3.56 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000 loops each)
}}}

Proposed

{{{#!py
In [2]: %timeit geometry.tuple
212 μs ± 3.05 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000 loops each)
}}}

A 1.4x improvement.

ticket_data.title: Include the database alias in connection-failure error messages
ticket_data.description:
= Description =

When a project configures more than one entry in `DATABASES`, a failed
connection raises `django.db.utils.OperationalError` whose message comes
straight from the database driver and only mentions host and port:

{{{
django.db.utils.OperationalError: connection failed: connection to server
    at "127.0.0.1", port 5432 failed: Connection refused
}}}

Nothing in the exception identifies ''which'' database alias failed
(`default` vs any other entry in `DATABASES`), nor the configured `NAME`,
`USER`, or `HOST` for that alias. In a multi-database setup the same
host:port may be correct for one alias and wrong for another, so the reader
cannot tell which connection string was actually attempted. This is
especially painful when host/credentials come from environment variables —
a stale or overridden `*_HOST` can silently point `default` at localhost
while a second alias points at a remote server, and the error gives no hint
which of the two failed.

== Reproduction ==

{{{#!python
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        "NAME": "app",
        "USER": "app",
        "HOST": "localhost",   # nothing listening here
        "PORT": 5432,
    },
    "ecomdb": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        "NAME": "etx_ecom",
        "USER": "report_api",
        "HOST": "192.168.80.72",
        "PORT": 5432,
    },
}

User.objects.get_by_natural_key("alice")        # uses 'default'
EcomRecords.objects.using("ecomdb").exists()    # uses 'ecomdb'
}}}

Whichever connection fails, the raised message has the same shape; the only
way to know which alias was involved is to read the traceback back to the
call site and cross-check `connections[alias].settings_dict` manually.

= Proposal =

Enrich the error as it propagates out of
`BaseDatabaseWrapper.ensure_connection()` / `connect()` /
`get_new_connection()` so the driver error is reported together with the
connection alias and the key settings for that alias, e.g.:

{{{
django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to database 'ecomdb'
    (postgresql 'etx_ecom' at 192.168.80.72:5432 as 'report_api'):
    connection failed: connection to server at "127.0.0.1",
    port 5432 failed: Connection refused
}}}

An alternative or complementary approach is to attach the context
programmatically instead of only in the message text — e.g.
`BaseException.add_note()` (Python 3.11+) or an attribute such as
`exc.django_connection_alias = self.alias` — so that logging,
error-reporting tools, and tests can pick the alias up without parsing the
message.

= Notes =

 * `django.db.backends.signals.connection_created` exists for ''successful''
   connections, but there is no equivalent signal or hook on failure. Today
   the only way to add the alias is to subclass each backend's
   `DatabaseWrapper` under a custom `ENGINE` path — which also means the
   workaround must be re-implemented per third-party backend rather than once
   in Django itself.
 * Care should be taken not to include the connection `PASSWORD` in the
   enriched message; `NAME`/`USER`/`HOST`/`PORT` are already visible in
   `settings_dict` and match what drivers print today.

ticket_data.title: Update, Move, Consolidate, Archive, or Remove Cookbook Wiki page from Trac?
ticket_data.description:
I was reading a deep cut forum post and someone linked to Django's Cookbook Wiki (https://code.djangoproject.com/wiki/CookBook). 

I haven't looked through all the links, but a few things jumped out at me at first glance on the main table of contents page as potentials to update:
- Text at the top that says "Can someone 'in the know' please check which recipes are still relevant? Thanks."
- Two broken links:
  - FreeComment app?
  - Making User info available outside requests?

Relatedly, I'm not sure about how much this is used (or updated) by others. If it's still useful as a common reference, we might consider improving its discoverability in some way, e.g. consolidating these into the main documentation site or moving them there wholesale. This is one of the only times I've come across it, and I've poked around the Django community a decent amount. 

Alternatively, if they're not useful or out of date, updating, archiving or removing them might be considered. 

PS: when I went to copy/paste the link for the Cookbook page in this ticket, I found that I actually couldn't get to it from the "Wiki" tab in the top menu (I previously expected that I could and they were the same because when you're on the Cookbook page, the menu looks like its selecting "Wiki" in dark green). So the Wiki page (https://code.djangoproject.com/wiki) is both not the Cookbook page and also doesn't link to the Cookbook page either. This might be because it's been intentionally or unintentionally pseudo-archived in the past by removing links to it. If that was intentional, we might consider adding a note at the top of the Cookbook page that gives a heads up to stray wanderers that it's archived and not being maintained/updated.

ticket_data.title: Document which constraints model formsets validate across forms
ticket_data.description:
Model formsets validate unique, unique_together, unique_for_date|month|year, and UniqueConstraints with fields and no condition across forms in the formset (#9493, #30581). This is only mentioned in passing, in [https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/forms/modelforms/#overriding-clean-on-a-modelformset Overriding clean() on a ModelFormSet], as the reason to call `super().clean()`. That passage lists only the first three. The `UniqueConstraint` support added in #30581 was never documented for formsets.

The docs also don't say:
- that `violation_error_message` isn't used for cross-form errors; a generic "Please correct the duplicate data for …" message is shown instead;
- that other constraints (conditional or expression-based `UniqueConstraint`s, `ExclusionConstraint`) are checked only against existing rows, not across forms, so saving can raise `IntegrityError`.

[https://github.com/django/django/pull/19249 PR]

Thanks Tim Schilling for the nudge to revive this work.

ticket_data.title: Add AddUniqueConstraintConcurrently and RemoveUniqueConstraintConcurrently operations for PostgreSQL
ticket_data.description:
See the [https://github.com/django/new-features/issues/124 new feature proposal] for a full discussion.

`AddIndexConcurrently` and `RemoveIndexConcurrently` let `Meta.indexes` entries be created and dropped without locking writes to the table, but `UniqueConstraint` in `Meta.constraints` has no equivalent. Many `UniqueConstraint`s are built as `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` (those with `expressions`, `condition`, `include`, or `opclasses`), so they can use `CONCURRENTLY` directly.

The proposal is to add `AddUniqueConstraintConcurrently` and `RemoveUniqueConstraintConcurrently` to `django.contrib.postgres.operations`, with `atomic = False` and the same in-transaction check as the existing concurrent index operations.

There's an open question about what to do with plain `fields=[...]` constraints, which are created with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE`. The options are:
 1. Build the index with `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, then attach it with `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... UNIQUE USING INDEX`, which only takes a brief lock. This is the approach used by [https://django-pg-migration-tools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage/operations.html#SaferAddUniqueConstraint django-pg-migration-tools].
 2. Raise an error.
 3. Fall back to the non-concurrent behavior (the original proposal).

Option 1 would allow covering every `UniqueConstraint`.

ticket_data.title: Django 6.1: TypeError in Query.add_select_col() when combining QuerySets with Meta.ordering referencing related model fields
ticket_data.description:
The following problem occurs with Django 6.1, PostgreSQL, Python 3.14.

For a model (with a regular primary key) and Meta.ordering referencing fields through a foreign key (`ordering = ('user__lastname', )`, say), QuerySet.difference() applied to two QuerySets of that model (e.g., as a trivial example, `A.objects.all().difference(A.objects.all())`) throws a TypeError during SQL compilation because query.selected is None.

Adding .order_by() without arguments to the difference method resolves the problem.

The same query worked in Django 6.0. The problem might be related to #37466

Thanks for your work.

ticket_data.title: Oracle "executemany()" fails with mixed-length strings in Django 6.1.3, but works in Django 6.1.2
ticket_data.description:
== Description ==

I encountered a regression after upgrading Django from 6.1.2 to 6.1.3.

I use `cursor.executemany()` to insert data into an Oracle table. One of the columns is defined as `VARCHAR2(8000)` and some values exceed 4000 characters.

The same code works with Django 6.1.2 but fails with Django 6.1.3.

== Environment ==

 * Django: 6.1.3 (works with 6.1.2)
 * python-oracledb: 26.1.0
 * Oracle database with `MAX_STRING_SIZE=EXTENDED`
 * Target column: `VARCHAR2(8000)`

== Steps to reproduce ==

Create a table:

{{{
CREATE TABLE django_lob_test (
    id NUMBER(10) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    text_value VARCHAR2(8000)
);
}}}

Run the following code using Django's database connection:

{{{#!python
from django.db import connection

small_text = "s" * 3500
large_text = "L" * 4199

rows = [
    [100, small_text],
    [101, large_text],
]

with connection.cursor() as cursor:
    cursor.executemany(
        "INSERT INTO django_lob_test (id, text_value) VALUES (%s, %s)",
        rows,
    )
}}}

== Actual results ==

With Django 6.1.3, the operation fails with:

{{{
oracledb.exceptions.NotSupportedError:
DPY-3013: unsupported Python type LOB for database type DB_TYPE_VARCHAR
}}}

Reversing the order of the rows produces a different error:

{{{
oracledb.exceptions.NotSupportedError:
DPY-3013: unsupported Python type str for database type DB_TYPE_CLOB
}}}

== Additional tests ==

I also tested the same inserts using the native python-oracledb cursor:

{{{#!python
raw_cursor = connection.connection.cursor()

raw_cursor.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO django_lob_test (id, text_value) VALUES (:1, :2)",
    rows,
)

raw_cursor.close()
}}}

Both row orders work successfully with the native cursor:

 * Short string first, long string second: SUCCESS
 * Long string first, short string second: SUCCESS

The issue does not occur with Django 6.1.2.

== Possible relation to #37411 ==

I noticed that Django 6.1.3 includes the fix for [https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/37411 #37411 – Add support for python-oracledb version 26].

Looking at the changes in that ticket, I noticed that `OracleParam` now converts strings longer than 4000 bytes into temporary LOB objects using `cursor.connection.createlob()`.

I wonder if this change could be related to the issue, as the batch appears to contain a mixture of regular Python strings and LOB objects. I have not investigated the Django implementation in enough detail to confirm this, but thought it might be a useful starting point.

ticket_data.title: FETCH_PEERS: GenericForeignKey returns a stale object after changing object_id or content_type
ticket_data.description:
With `FETCH_PEERS`, a `GenericForeignKey` keeps returning the old object after its `object_id` or `content_type` changes.

Models:

{{{#!python
from django.contrib.contenttypes.fields import GenericForeignKey
from django.contrib.contenttypes.models import ContentType
from django.db import models


class Author(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)


class Book(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    author = models.ForeignKey(Author, models.CASCADE)


class Tag(models.Model):
    content_type = models.ForeignKey(ContentType, models.CASCADE)
    object_id = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    content_object = GenericForeignKey()
}}}

{{{#!python
alice = Author.objects.create(name="Alice")
bob = Author.objects.create(name="Bob")
Tag.objects.create(content_object=alice)
Tag.objects.create(content_object=alice)

tag1, tag2 = Tag.objects.fetch_mode(FETCH_PEERS).order_by("pk")
tag1.content_object
tag1.object_id = bob.pk
tag1.content_object.name
}}}

This returns `'Alice'`. With `FETCH_ONE` it returns `'Bob'`.

Changing the content type is worse. After setting `tag1.content_type` to `Book` and `tag1.object_id` to a book's pk, `tag1.content_object` still returns the `Author`, an object of the wrong model.

Cause: `GenericForeignKeyDescriptor.__get__()` sees that the cached object no longer matches, but it doesn't clear the cache before calling `fetch()`. `fetch_many()` skips every instance that has a cached value, including this one, so nothing is fetched and the stale object is returned.

Clearing the cache with `self.field.delete_cached_value(instance)` before fetching fixes it. I can submit a patch with a test if this is accepted.

ticket_data.title: Parallel test runner should report failure for work interrupted on a dead worker
ticket_data.description:
When manually testing the fix for #27734 (06463d3c11b3ce132075283d5f9368a269d66343), we engineered parallel test workers to die by creating them with `maxtasksperchild=1`. ticket_data.title: Gunicorn now complains about HEAD responses with bodies
ticket_data.description:
This is a boundary issues between Django and Gunicorn resulting from changes in Gunicorn 26.1.0.

Way back in version 1.9, Django dropped its behavior of removing bodies in responses to HEAD requests on the basis that most WSGI servers already did that work.  See https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/26052

Gunicorn 26.1.0 introduced warning logging when the application includes a body in responses to HEAD requests.  See https://github.com/benoitc/gunicorn/commit/9bc5891b4b06f25a8ce0e707053dcb2fb9bf638c

As a result, logs now get polluted with these warnings.  Gunicorn doesn't offer a simple way to control that warning (would need to craft a custom logging configuration to target the warning for exclusion).

As an application owner, Gunicorn is signalling that applications returning bodies to HEAD requests are a "problem to be solved by the application."  But Django explicitly removed this behavior because it was redundant with the common WSGI server implementations.

I don't know if either side is more correct than the other, but a conversation between the Django and Gunicorn teams is probably the most effective way to find a user-friendly resolution.  Otherwise each project can point the finger back at the other and the user experience will suffer indefinitely.

ticket_data.title: UserAdmin allows adding users without change permission through _saveasnew
ticket_data.description:
`UserAdmin` requires both add and change permissions to create users. See https://github.com/django/django/blob/9e2e5a31e2ef2e8673d3c2a38d2a391dbf42cf23/django/contrib/auth/admin.py#L122-L129

However, the additional change permission check can be bypassed by posting to a user’s change URL with `_saveasnew`.
The POST is processed even with the default `save_as=False`.

Here is a test to show the behavior:

{{{#!diff
--- a/tests/auth_tests/test_views.py
+++ b/tests/auth_tests/test_views.py
@@ -1507,6 +1507,28 @@ class ChangelistTests(MessagesTestMixin, AuthViewsTestCase):
             )
         self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 400)
 
+    def test_save_as_new_requires_change_permission(self):
+        user = User.objects.create_user(username="add_only", is_staff=True)
+        add_permission = Permission.objects.get(codename="add_user")
+        user.user_permissions.add(add_permission)
+        self.client.force_login(user)
+
+        data = {
+            "username": "new_user",
+            "usable_password": "true",
+            "password1": "a-long-test-password-123",
+            "password2": "a-long-test-password-123",
+            "_saveasnew": "Save as new",
+        }
+        for url in [
+            reverse("admin:auth_user_add"),
+            reverse("admin:auth_user_change", args=[user.pk])
+        ]:
+            with self.subTest(url=url):
+                response = self.client.post(url, data)
+                self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 403)
+                self.assertFalse(User.objects.filter(username="new_user").exists())
+
     def test_user_change_email(self):
         data = self.get_user_data(self.admin)
}}}

This was reviewed by the Django Security Team and is being handled as a permissions consistency bug rather than a security issue. With the default UserAdmin, this path still uses the restricted user creation form: submitted privilege fields such as is_superuser are ignored, and the created account is an ordinary user.

ticket_data.title: DomainNameValidator accepts Unicode line/paragraph separators in domains
ticket_data.description:
`django/core/validators.py` builds `hostname_re` / `domain_re` / `tld_re` using the raw codepoint range `[a-z\u00a1-\uffff0-9-]`. That range includes
Unicode line and paragraph separators and several invisible space characters (U+2028, U+2029, U+1680, U+2000–200A, U+3000, U+FEFF), so they are accepted whenever they appear in a non-final domain label.

`EmailValidator` and `URLValidator` reuse these regexes, so `EmailField.is_valid()` returns `True` for such values.

Two consequences:

1. `send_mail()` on a validated address raises an uncaught `ValueError` ("Header values may not contain linefeed or carriage return characters") from Python's `email.policy` serialization. `PasswordResetForm.send_mail` swallows it via a broad `except Exception`; other callers surface it as a 500.
1. `django/core/mail/backends/smtp.py` `prep_address()` silently strips the separators, so the envelope recipient differs from the validated address (`user@example\u2028.com` → `user@example.com`).

POC script and its output attached.

== Suggested fix
In `DomainNameValidator.__call__()`, reject characters whose `unicodedata.category(ch)[0]` is `C` or `Z`, or narrow the `\u00a1-\uffff` range to actual letter/digit categories. This covers `EmailValidator`, `URLValidator`, and `simple_url_2_re` consumers.

Regression cases: `user@example\u2028.com`, `exa\u1680mple.com`, `http://example\u2029.com/`.

== Acknowledgement
This was a report received by the security team. The reporter did not respond when asked to open a ticket, so I'm opening it. I edited the report a little.

ticket_data.title: Removing unique_together in the same migration as CreateModel drops a pending index, or crashes with KeyError: 'columns'
ticket_data.description:
Since cd385e6b8c16b51f68c1f220ff09a4cfd679af0c (#31317, backported to 6.1 as 622aabce56), `BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._delete_composed_index()` first looks in `deferred_sql` for the unique_together statement. It removes the first `Statement` on the table that references all the columns and whose `parts["columns"]` match. It does not check that this statement is the unique_together one. An index or foreign key on the same column is also a deferred statement on that column, so:

 * a pending `db_index` (or foreign key) index is removed from `deferred_sql` and never created, and the real unique constraint stays in the database;
 * a pending foreign key constraint has a `column` part, not `columns`, so `deferred.parts["columns"]` raises `KeyError: 'columns'` on PostgreSQL.

This needs CreateModel, AlterUniqueTogether (add) and AlterUniqueTogether (remove) in one migration, for example a hand-written or squashed migration (a RunPython between them stops the optimizer from merging them).

Reproduction (`tests/migrations/test_operations.py` style):

{{{#!python
self.apply_operations(
    "test_aluntodi",
    ProjectState(),
    operations=[
        migrations.CreateModel(
            "Pony",
            fields=[
                ("id", models.AutoField(primary_key=True)),
                ("weight", models.IntegerField(db_index=True)),
            ],
        ),
        migrations.AlterUniqueTogether(name="Pony", unique_together={("weight",)}),
        migrations.AlterUniqueTogether(name="Pony", unique_together=set()),
    ],
)
}}}

Actual (SQLite and PostgreSQL): there is no index on `weight`, and the unique constraint on `weight` is still there.

Expected: a plain index on `weight` and no unique constraint, as in Django 6.0.

With `stable = models.ForeignKey("test_aluntodfk.Stable", models.CASCADE)` instead of `weight`, PostgreSQL raises:

{{{
  File "django/db/backends/base/schema.py", line 679, in _delete_composed_index
    and deferred.parts["columns"].columns == columns
        ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^
KeyError: 'columns'
}}}

On SQLite the foreign key index is dropped and the unique constraint stays, as above.

Versions: main and 6.1.0 to 6.1.3. 6.0.x works.

Regression in cd385e6b8c16b51f68c1f220ff09a4cfd679af0c. A reviewer on PR 20929 suggested guarding the `columns` lookup; that guard was not merged, and it would fix only the crash, not the dropped index.

Suggested fix: only remove the statement that `create_model()` deferred for unique_together, i.e. one whose `name` part is the `_uniq` `IndexName` that `_unique_constraint_name()` builds. A patch with tests for both cases follows.

AI disclosure: I found and reproduced this with Claude Code (Anthropic).

ticket_data.title: ~F() on a nullable BooleanField maps NULL to False on SQLite
ticket_data.description:
On SQLite, negating a nullable `BooleanField` with `~F()` turns `NULL` into `False`. So `update(flag=~F("flag"))`, the documented way to swap a boolean, overwrites `NULL` values with `False`, and `exclude(~F("flag"))` returns rows where `flag` is `NULL`.

Django 6.0 on SQLite and every version on PostgreSQL keep `NULL`, as SQL `NOT NULL` does.

{{{#!python
class Item(models.Model):
    flag = models.BooleanField(null=True)
}}}

{{{#!python
Item.objects.create(flag=True)
Item.objects.create(flag=False)
Item.objects.create(flag=None)

Item.objects.annotate(n=~F("flag")).order_by("pk").values_list("n", flat=True)
# Actual: [False, True, False]    Expected: [False, True, None]

Item.objects.exclude(~F("flag")).values_list("flag", flat=True)
# Actual: [True, None]            Expected: [True]

Item.objects.update(flag=~F("flag"))
Item.objects.order_by("pk").values_list("flag", flat=True)
# Actual: [False, True, False]    Expected: [False, True, None]
}}}

Cause: since 4bbc27c8686f10f9556cef02dbfa9f5157fbcf56 (#36492, backported to 6.1), `conditional_expression_supported_in_where_clause()` returns `False` on SQLite for a plain column, so `NegatedExpression.as_sql()` emits `CASE WHEN flag = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END` instead of `NOT flag`. The `ELSE 0` branch catches `NULL`.

Versions: 6.1 and main on SQLite (regression in 4bbc27c8686f10f9556cef02dbfa9f5157fbcf56). MySQL and Oracle have used the same `CASE` since `~F()` was added in 4.2 (a320aab5129f4019b3c1d28b7a3b509582bc56f9), so they have the same bug; I read those code paths but did not run them.

Suggested fix: keep `NULL` in the `CASE`: `CASE WHEN flag = 0 THEN 1 WHEN flag <> 0 THEN 0 END`. This matches `NOT` for all three values, keeps the #36492 change to exact lookups against literals, and fixes MySQL and Oracle too. The cost is that the negated SQL (and its params) appears twice.

AI disclosure: I found and reproduced this with Claude Code (Anthropic).

ticket_data.title: HttpResponse.delete_cookie() matches cookie name prefixes case-sensitively
ticket_data.description:
`HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` adds the `Secure` flag when the cookie name starts with `__Secure-`, `__Host-` or `__Http-`, and the `HttpOnly` flag when it starts with `__Http-` or `__Host-Http-` (#28989, #37467). It compares the prefixes case-sensitively:

{{{#!python
secure = key.startswith(("__Secure-", "__Host-", "__Http-")) or (...)
httponly = key.startswith(("__Http-", "__Host-Http-"))
}}}

User agents match these prefixes case-insensitively. draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22, section 5.4 ("Cookie Name Prefixes"): "UAs MUST match the prefix string case-insensitively", and section 5.7 ("Storage Model"), steps 20 and 21: "If the cookie-name begins with a case-insensitive match for the string "__Secure-", abort this algorithm and ignore the cookie entirely unless the cookie's secure-only-flag is true." draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-02, section 5.4.3 ("Store a Cookie"), steps 13 to 16, does the same for `__Secure-`, `__Host-`, `__Http-` and `__Host-Http-`: "If cookie's name, byte-lowercased, starts with __secure- and cookie's secure is false, then return null."

So a browser treats a cookie named `__host-sid` or `__SECURE-sid` as prefixed, but Django deletes it without `Secure` (or without `HttpOnly` for `__http-`), and the browser ignores the deletion. The cookie stays.

Reproduction:

{{{#!python
from django.conf import settings
settings.configure()
from django.http import HttpResponse

r = HttpResponse()
for name in ("__host-sid", "__SECURE-sid", "__http-sid", "__host-http-sid"):
    r.delete_cookie(name)
    print(r.cookies[name].output())
}}}

Actual:
{{{
Set-Cookie: __host-sid=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/
Set-Cookie: __SECURE-sid=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/
Set-Cookie: __http-sid=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/
Set-Cookie: __host-http-sid=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/
}}}

Expected: `Secure` on all four, and `HttpOnly` on the last two, as Django already does for `__Host-sid`, `__Secure-sid`, `__Http-sid` and `__Host-Http-sid`.

Versions affected: every version since the prefix check was added in #28989 (Django 2.1); #37467 (308b6d6ac0, main only) added `__Http-` and `__Host-Http-` with the same case-sensitive match. Not a regression.

`set_cookie()` has no prefix logic, so only `delete_cookie()` is affected.

Suggested fix: compare against the lowercased name:

{{{#!python
lower_key = key.lower()
secure = lower_key.startswith(("__secure-", "__host-", "__http-")) or (...)
httponly = lower_key.startswith(("__http-", "__host-http-"))
}}}

ticket_data.title: XOR fallback treats NULL operands as false, so filter() and exclude() can return the same row
ticket_data.description:
On databases without a native `XOR` (`supports_logical_xor = False`: SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle), `WhereNode.as_sql()` rewrites `a ^ b ^ ...` as `(a OR b OR ...) AND 1 = MOD(CASE WHEN a THEN 1 ELSE 0 END + ..., 2)`. The `ELSE 0` counts a `NULL` (unknown) operand as false. As a result:

 * `exclude(q)` can return rows that `filter(q)` also returns.
 * `filter(q)` returns rows that MariaDB and MySQL do not, since their native `XOR` gives `NULL` when either side is `NULL`.

{{{#!python
class Number(models.Model):
    num = models.IntegerField(null=True)
    other_num = models.IntegerField()
}}}

{{{#!python
for num, other_num in [(1, 1), (2, 1), (None, 1), (1, 2), (None, 2)]:
    Number.objects.create(num=num, other_num=other_num)  # pks 1-5

q = ~Q(num=1) ^ Q(other_num=1)
Number.objects.filter(q)   # pks [1, 5]
Number.objects.exclude(q)  # Actual: [2, 4, 5]    Expected: [2, 4]

Number.objects.filter(Q(num=1) ^ Q(other_num=1))
# Actual: [2, 3, 4]    MySQL: [2, 4]
}}}

Row 5 is in both `filter(q)` and `exclude(q)`. In `exclude(q)` the operand `~Q(num=1)` compiles to `NOT (num = 1)`, which is `NULL` for row 5. The fallback counts it as 0, so the `XOR` is false and `exclude()` keeps the row. MySQL gives `NULL XOR FALSE = NULL` and drops it.

Versions: every version since `XOR` support landed in 4.1 (c6b4d62fa2, #29865); #34604 (b81e974e9e) changed the sum to a parity check but kept `ELSE 0`. Reproduced on main on SQLite and PostgreSQL 16; stable/6.1.x and stable/6.0.x have the same code. Not a regression.

Suggested fix: map each operand to `CASE WHEN c THEN 1 WHEN NOT c THEN 0 END`, so a `NULL` operand makes the sum, and the `XOR`, `NULL`. For any number of operands this matches native `XOR` and SQL three-valued logic, and `filter(q)` and `exclude(q)` can no longer overlap.

This is a trade-off that needs a decision. Today a plain `XOR` without `~` splits rows cleanly between `filter()` and `exclude()`, because `exclude()` adds `IS NOT NULL` to each operand. With the fix, a `NULL` operand makes the row match neither, as on MySQL. For example, `Q(num__isnull=True) ^ Q(num=1)` ("num is NULL or 1, but not both") matches rows 3 and 5 today and matches neither of them with the fix, nor on MySQL. The fix also changes annotations (`annotate(x=Q(num=1) ^ Q(other_num=1))` gives `None` for row 3 instead of `True`) and check constraints (`CheckConstraint(condition=Q(num=1) ^ Q(other_num=1))` stops rejecting rows where `num` is `NULL`; constraints already in the database keep the old SQL). The other choice is to keep two-valued operands and fix `exclude()` instead, which keeps the results we have today but leaves these databases out of step with MySQL.

The operand's SQL and params then appear three times (once in the `OR`, twice in the `CASE`) instead of twice, so a subquery operand may run more often.

Related: #37520 is adding a shared NULL-keeping template, `CASE WHEN {sql} THEN 1 WHEN NOT ({sql}) THEN 0 END`, for `NegatedExpression`, `Lookup`/`WhereNode.select_format()` and `GeneratedField`. The `XOR` fallback is a separate case (a sum of operands in `WHERE`), but it could use the same template once that lands.

I have a patch with tests for the suggested fix ready. Django's PR limit stops me from opening a PR while my earlier ones ([https://github.com/django/django/pull/21642 PR 21642], [https://github.com/django/django/pull/22007 PR 22007], [https://github.com/django/django/pull/22247 PR 22247]) are open, so I'll open it as soon as one of them is merged and the approach is agreed.

ticket_data.title: Model formsets raise TypeError with sliced querysets ordered by a non-unique field
ticket_data.description:
Model formsets raise `TypeError: Cannot reorder a query once a slice has been taken.` when given a sliced queryset ordered by a non-unique field.

This worked in Django 6.0.10, but fails in 6.1, 6.1.3, and on main at `c67d872765`.

To reproduce, use an `Author` model with a non-unique `name` field and run the following against an empty table:

{{{
#!python
from django.forms import modelformset_factory
for name in ["Walt", "Charles", "Arthur", "Paul"]:
    Author.objects.create(name=name)
AuthorFormSet = modelformset_factory(Author, fields=["name"], extra=0)
formset = AuthorFormSet(queryset=Author.objects.order_by("name")[1:3])
[form.instance.name for form in formset.forms]
}}}

Expected result: `["Charles", "Paul"]`, preserving the order of the supplied queryset.

Actual result: `TypeError: Cannot reorder a query once a slice has been taken.`

I traced the regression to [https://github.com/django/django/commit/856c915326768962806705ca7733e4abbb8f794f 856c915326], introduced for #37004. The change makes `BaseModelFormSet.get_queryset()` append `pk` when the queryset isn’t totally ordered. For sliced querysets, this triggers an `order_by()` call after the slice, which Django doesn’t allow.

I confirmed this with a SQLite regression test that passes on the parent of that commit and fails on the commit itself.

I’ve also prepared a patch on my fork.

The regression test fails on main at `c67d872765` and passes with the patch on both SQLite and PostgreSQL 18.6. Both model formset test modules also pass on PostgreSQL.

If the ticket is accepted, I’ll open a pull request with the fix.

I used OpenAI Codex with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol to investigate and reproduce the regression, prepare the patch, and run the tests.

ticket_data.title: GDALRaster._preprocess_input doesn't handle RecursionError from deeply nested JSON
ticket_data.description:
== Problem ==

`GDALRaster._preprocess_input` (django/contrib/gis/gdal/raster/source.py:243)
calls `json.loads(ds_input)` without catching `RecursionError`. While Python's
json C parser is mostly iterative, `json.loads()` may still raise
`RecursionError` rather than `JSONDecodeError` when input nesting exceeds the
interpreter's recursion limit (the same behavior that motivated the fix in
#37491 / CVE-2026-114582 for `ExternalCRSBlocker.check()` in
django/contrib/gis/gdal/geojson.py).

== Sibling already fixed ==

`ExternalCRSBlocker.check()` was patched 9 days ago (commit d3954c9, Nov 12)
to catch `RecursionError` and reraise as `ValueError("GeoJSON input is nested
too deeply.")`. The form fields `JSONField` and `HStoreField` also catch
`RecursionError` (tests/forms_tests/field_tests/test_jsonfield.py:33-39 and
tests/postgres_tests/test_hstore.py:377-382).

`GDALRaster._preprocess_input` is the direct sibling in the same module area
and missed the same treatment.

== Proposed fix ==

Wrap `json.loads(ds_input)` in `try/except RecursionError` and reraise as
`ValueError("Raster JSON input is nested too deeply.")`, mirroring the
geojson.py fix.

== Reproduction ==

Constructing `GDALRaster(deeply_nested_json_string)` (e.g. via direct API
call or any code path that passes attacker-controlled JSON to GDALRaster)
currently propagates an uncaught `RecursionError` to the caller. With the
proposed fix, callers receive a `ValueError` they can handle as a bad-input
condition (the form field already catches `ValueError`).

calls `json.loads(ds_input)` without catching `RecursionError`. While Python's
json C parser is mostly iterative, `json.loads()` may still raise
`RecursionError` rather than `JSONDecodeError` when input nesting exceeds the
interpreter's recursion limit (the same behavior that motivated the fix in
#37491 / CVE-2026-114582 for `ExternalCRSBlocker.check()` in
django/contrib/gis/gdal/geojson.py).

== Sibling already fixed ==

`ExternalCRSBlocker.check()` was patched 9 days ago (commit d3954c9, Nov 12)
to catch `RecursionError` and reraise as `ValueError("GeoJSON input is nested
too deeply.")`. The form fields `JSONField` and `HStoreField` also catch
`RecursionError` (tests/forms_tests/field_tests/test_jsonfield.py:33-39 and
tests/postgres_tests/test_hstore.py:377-382).

`GDALRaster._preprocess_input` is the direct sibling in the same module area
and missed the same treatment.

== Proposed fix ==

Wrap `json.loads(ds_input)` in `try/except RecursionError` and reraise as
`ValueError("Raster JSON input is nested too deeply.")`, mirroring the
geojson.py fix.

== Reproduction ==

Constructing `GDALRaster(deeply_nested_json_string)` (e.g. via direct API
call or any code path that passes attacker-controlled JSON to GDALRaster)
currently propagates an uncaught `RecursionError` to the caller. With the
proposed fix, callers receive a `ValueError` they can handle as a bad-input
condition (the form field already catches `ValueError`).

ticket_data.title: Model._perform_unique_checks() uses the default connection's features instead of the routed database's
ticket_data.description:
`Model._perform_unique_checks()` decides whether to skip a lookup for an empty string using `connection.features.interprets_empty_strings_as_nulls`, where `connection` is the default database connection.

However, the uniqueness query that follows is routed through `DATABASE_ROUTERS` (via `model_class._default_manager.db`). When reads are routed to a database whose backend differs from the default one (for example Oracle alongside PostgreSQL), the empty-string check uses the wrong backend's behavior, so validation can skip or run the uniqueness query incorrectly.

There was already a `TODO: Handle multiple backends with different feature flags` at that spot. Other code, such as `UniqueConstraint.validate()` and related managers, already resolves `features` from the routed database alias.

Steps to reproduce: configure two databases with different values of `features.interprets_empty_strings_as_nulls`, add a router whose `db_for_read()` returns the non-default alias, and call `validate_unique()` on an instance with an empty string in a unique `CharField`. Whether the query runs depends on the default database rather than the routed one.

Patch: https://github.com/nehmtech/django/tree/unique-checks-routed-db-features
